request.system:
You are assisting with the qualitative analysis of interview data from a study of frontline hotel employees' work experiences. You will receive one passage from an interview transcript. Code the passage as a qualitative researcher would in first-order coding, and complete the coding form below.

About the passage
- The passage begins with brief details about the interviewee: role, gender and years in the job.
- Lines marked "Interviewer:" are the interviewer's questions. Lines marked "Interviewee:" are the interviewee's answers.
- Some passages contain two excerpts from the same interview, marked [Earlier in the interview] and [Later in the interview].

The coding form
1. codes: Give between 3 and 6 first-order codes. Each code has a short label of 2 to 6 words, kept close to the interviewee's own language, and one supporting quote. Each quote must be copied word for word from the passage, without any change, and must be no longer than 30 words.
2. interpretation: In one or two sentences, in your own words, state what the interviewee is communicating in this passage.
3. tone: The overall tone of the interviewee's account. Choose one: positive, negative, mixed or neutral.
4. confidence: An integer from 0 to 100 indicating how confident you are that your interpretation is accurate.

Respond only with a JSON object that follows the schema provided. Write in English.
request.user:
Interviewee details: Concierge team leader, male, 12th year

Interviewer: You’ve been here twelve years and seen several general managers come and go. What do you think of the current one?

Interviewee: The current one? He’s all right, I suppose. Nothing out of the ordinary. He doesn’t have much contact with us on the front line. If we run into him in the lobby, he nods. The year before last my son had an operation, and things were pretty hard at home around that time. I took leave through the normal procedure. HR approved half a month, the union gave me a 2,000-yuan support payment as the rules provide, and my colleagues in the department chipped in a bit too. There are set rules for all of that. It has nothing to do with which general manager is in charge. My son’s doing well now. He’s at junior high, and he’s taller than me. He had his mid-term exams last month and got 98 in maths. I took a photo of his report and sent it to a whole lot of relatives. At this year’s annual party, the general manager came over to our table to make a toast. He said a few words about our hard work and everyone raised their glasses. I was drinking a soft drink, he didn’t pay any attention, and he turned and went on to the next table. There used to be a money tree outside his office door. Later it withered and Admin replaced it with a new one. I only heard that from other people. We don’t usually go up to that floor. My colleagues say he’s capable when it comes to running the business. Occupancy is a bit higher than under the last one. He’s just a bit distant from us, and all he talks about in meetings is numbers. In all my years here, I’ve probably said no more than ten sentences to him altogether. To be honest, it doesn’t make much difference to us who the general manager is. What matters to us is mainly the department manager. Anyway, he’s a competent leader. Just write that. If you want to know about the concierge team’s work, you can ask about other things, like how we book cars and restaurants for guests. I can explain all that clearly.
